decisions.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt In the current study, we attempted to replicate the primary result of Study 5from Reynolds & Besner (2008), wherein there was no delay in responding when switching between stimulus categories while reading words and nonwords aloud. This effect was produced at two levels of analysis – participant-level, and stimulus item-level. In our replication with high power and a similar sample, we partially replicated the original results. We conducted both participant- level and item-level analyses and found that there was no significant evidence for a switch cost at the participant-level, but there was a switch cost when the data was analyzed at an item level. Lastly, there was an unexpected interaction between switch cost and stimulus type (i.e., word or nonword) when the data was analyzed at the participant level but not at the stimulus item level. Participants read words more slowly after a switch, but read nonwords at a similar speed regardless of whether there was a switch. In contrast to the reaction-time results, we fully replicated the error rate results from Study 5.

Per Codebook Step 4 Rule 1, the authors' overall conclusion governs, and an explicitly partial verdict where some tested components succeed while others fail is coded 'mixed'. In the primary report for Reynolds & Besner (2008, Study 5), Simpson & Lai explicitly conclude that 'we partially replicated the original results': error rate analyses and the item-level interaction null (F(1, 92) = 1.95, p = .17) and participant-level switch-cost null (F(1, 19) = .03, p = .86) replicated, whereas an unexpected stimulus type x switch condition interaction emerged at the participant level (F(1, 19) = 4.77, p = .042) and a significant switch cost emerged at the item level (F(1, 92) = 5.62, p = .020). The shipped 'successful' coding relied solely on the single item-level interaction entry in the RPP spreadsheet rather than the primary report's overall partial verdict.

decisions.quote: Regarding the primary finding, we detected a statistically significant effect of nearness, F (1, 29) = 8.064, p = .008, partial η2 = .218, whereby words with many near neighbors were categorized more slowly than words with few near neighbors. We failed to detect a statistically significant effect for distant neighbors, F (1, 29) = 1.562, p = .221, partial η2 = .051. In addition, we failed to detect a statistically significant interaction effect, F (1, 29) = 3.192, p = .084, partial η2 = .099. Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt The present findings indicate a successful replication attempt in terms of statistical significance. Specifically, a statistically “significant” (i.e., p < .01) effect of nearness in the predicted direction was found in our replication study, replicating what was observed in the original study. However, the observed effect size in our replication (partial η2 = .22) was smaller than the effect size observed in the original study (partial η2 = .45).

Per Codebook Step 4 Rule 1 and the 'successful' definition, 'The authors' overall conclusion governs' and 'A finding the authors treat as supported is successful even when the effect is smaller or weaker than the original: effect size alone does not make it mixed.' In the primary report for Mirman & Magnuson (2008, Experiment 2), Bosco & Field identify the nearness main effect as the primary target finding (confirmed by the original authors), find it statistically significant in the predicted direction (F(1, 29) = 8.064, p = .008, partial η2 = .218), and explicitly conclude in their Summary of Replication Attempt that 'The present findings indicate a successful replication attempt in terms of statistical significance.' The shipped 'mixed' coding improperly downgraded a successful verdict solely because the replication effect size (partial η2 = .22) was smaller than the original (partial η2 = .45).

decisions.quote: Discussion The results from this replication largely matched the findings from the initial investigation, though the replication of the critical finding itself was mixed. Even with the critical finding, though the single-statistic interaction was not significant, the planned comparisons at each set size did support the initial authors’ claim that the retro-cue benefit exists at all set sizes except for set size 1. In addition to finding support for this principle, we ran the remainder of the same statistical sets as the original authors, and found similar results (see Figure comparing the replication and original). First, there was a main effect of cue type (retro cue > simultaneous cue) across memory set size as a whole [F(1,17) = 66.02, p < 0.0001], and as mentioned above, planned comparisons at each set size showed that this difference existed at all set sizes but set size 1. Moreover, there was an interaction between set size and cue type [F(1,17) = 3.19, p < 0.21], but no such interaction existed once set size 1 was removed from the analysis, providing additional evidence that set size 1 is the outlying set size, which does not exhibit the retro-cue effect [F(4,68) = 1.59, p = 0.21). Further analysis also resulted in full replications when it came to the main effects of stimulus type (accuracy was higher with color than with shape, F(1,17) = 89.92, p < 0.0001) and memory load (accuracy was higher with smaller loads over larger ones, F(5,85) = 180.46, p < 0.0001). Figure: The pattern of results is largely the same for the original and replication studies. In both cases, retro-cue performance is better than simultaneous-cue performance at all set sizes except for set size 1, and the magnitude of this benefit is largely consistent across set size within a stimulus type. Interestingly, whereas in the original study the benefit provided by the retro-cue interacted only marginally with memory load when set size 1 was included, the effect was much more robust here. We suspect this can be accounted for by the larger sample size (18 > 12). It is also important to note that due to simultaneous key strokes, certain trial data was occasionally shifted in the experiment program and manual error correction was necessary. This occurred in a total of 5 trials across all participants. The overall success of replication helps in accumulating further evidence for the retro-cue phenomenon.

Per Codebook Step 4 Rule 1, 'Where the authors state an OVERALL verdict on the replication, that verdict decides the outcome, even where individual results point elsewhere. Do not override a clear overall verdict with a count of positive and negative sub-tests.' Although the single-statistic 2x2 interaction restricted to set sizes 1 and 2 was non-significant (F(1, 17) = 2.37, p = .142) so the authors noted that 'the replication of the critical finding itself was mixed', the planned comparisons across all set sizes (significant retro-cue benefit at set sizes 2-6, all ps < .01, and absent at set size 1, p = .259), the disappearance of the cue x set size interaction once set size 1 was removed, and the main effects of cue type, stimulus type, and memory load all replicated the original study. Accordingly, the replication authors explicitly state their overall verdict as 'The overall success of replication helps in accumulating further evidence for the retro-cue phenomenon' (and likewise recorded 'yes' for replication in the RPP master table, source_view.json line 1110).

decisions.quote: In regard to the list length, the result of the current study seems to only partially reflect that of the original study. Even though an effect of list length was identified, it was a moderate marginal trend, while the effect the original study was found to be significant. The sample size was the main difference between the current study (N = 21) and the original (N = 32). However, as based on our initial power analysis, it is unlikely to assume that this is the cause of the different results, as the estimated effect sizes of our analyses are quite a bit smaller than the effect sizes of the original study. The other main difference was the age of the participants. In the original study, participants were high school students, whereas in the current study the participants were first-year university students. It is unclear whether this could have affected the results. More research would be needed to explore the possible effects of age. Overall, the current study failed to replicate the specific results found in the original study in regard to the accuracy measures. However, while different, the current results do seem to be in line with the original paper’s conclusion favouring the Dual-Process Model.

All tested empirical accuracy effects from Oberauer (2008) failed to reach statistical significance in the replication (serial position x probe type quadratic trend in short-long group: F(1, 9) = 1.161, p = .309 vs. original p = .02; linear trend in long-short group: F(1, 10) = 1.485, p = .251 vs. original p = .006; list length main effect: F(1, 19) = 3.661, p = .071 vs. original p < .001). Although the authors briefly referred to the non-significant marginal trend for list length (p = .071) as 'partially replicated' in the summary paragraph, their explicit overall conclusion at the end of the report is: 'Overall, the current study failed to replicate the specific results found in the original study in regard to the accuracy measures.'

decisions.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt The findings from the present study indicate a successful replication in terms of statistical significance. Specifically, a statistically significant omnibus Group x Problem Type interaction for RT as well as percentage of errors was found in our replication, replicating what was observed in the original study. However, the same pattern of response time means during the test phase were not found, indicating that different processes could have driven the two significant omnibus interactions. Commentary Despite the replication of the significant omnibus ANOVA from experiment three of the original study, there were differences in the pattern of results between the original study and the present replication.

Per Codebook Step 4, 'mixed' applies when 'some tested hypotheses, studies, measures, conditions or sites succeed while others fail; ... a multi-part prediction is only partly borne out; or the authors' overall verdict is explicitly qualified or partial.' In their Analysis Plan (line 540), Ricker & Saide pre-specified a two-part criterion: 'in order for the replication attempt to be considered successful, we expect both the interaction to be significant as well as the pattern of cell means to follow those reported in the original paper.' While the omnibus Group x Problem Type interactions for test RT (F(2, 68) = 41.603, p < .001) and error rate (F(2, 68) = 4.993, p = .009), same-operation savings, and the practice RT Block x Operation interaction replicated, the critical operation-change RT savings pattern failed to replicate (74 ms and 1 ms vs. original 330 ms and 302 ms; practice error interaction also non-significant, p = .109), leading the authors to conclude that 'The discrepancy between patterns of means, and potentially the effect driving the significant interaction, calls into question whether the present study should truly be considered a successful replication' (line 545).

(2008, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 95, 510-523) Seung Kyung Kim Key Jung Lee skim2@stanford.edu keyjlee@stanford.edu Introduction The original paper by Albarracín et al. (2008) tested the hypothesis that general action and inaction goals can influence the amount of motor or cognitive output of various kinds. The authors conducted a series of experiments examining the effects of instilling general action and inaction goals using word primes, such as “action” and “rest.” We plan to replicate Experiment 5, which examined the effect of action and inaction primes on cognitive output.
